notes.title: Physics — Magnetism and Electromagnets
notes.text:
PHYSICS - MAGNETISM & ELECTROMAGNETS (topic 7)
Mr Okafor, Yr 10 set 2. revision for the end of topic test!!

== Magnets basics ==
- magnets have a north pole and a south pole. like poles repel, unlike (opposite) poles attract
- magnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt (and steel bc it has iron in it). NOT copper, NOT aluminium (my pencil case is aluminium & the magnet did nothing lol)
- permanent magnet = makes its own field all the time
- induced magnet = only becomes a magnet when its in a field. loses most of it when you take it out. ALWAYS ATTRACTS never repels (Mr O said this comes up every year)
- field lines go from N to S, closer together = stronger field. strongest at the poles

== Plotting compass practical ==
textbook p. 112 (the green AQA one)
- put bar magnet on paper, put plotting compass near the N end, mark where needle points, move compass to the dot, repeat... join dots up
- our field drawing was a bit wonky at the S end bc Josh kept knocking the table
- earth has a magnetic field too, thats why compasses work. the core is the reason (molten iron stuff)
- compass needle is basically a tiny magnet that lines up with the field

== Electromagnetism ==
- a wire with current through it has a magnetic field round it - circles around the wire
- RIGHT-HAND GRIP RULE: thumb = direction of current, curled fingers = direction of field
- bigger current = stronger field, further from wire = weaker
- solenoid = coil of wire. field inside is strong and uniform (same everywhere), outside looks like a bar magnet's field
- add an iron core -> electromagnet, way stronger
- electromagnets can be switched ON and OFF which is the whole point

== Our electromagnet practical (14th Oct) ==
group: "The Coil Gang" (me, Josh, Amira, Ben)
wound wire round an iron nail, connected to power pack at 2 A, counted how many paperclips it could pick up
| turns | paperclips |
| 10 | 4 |
| 20 | 9 |
| 30 | 13 |
| 40 | 17 |
- conclusion: more turns = stronger electromagnet, roughly proportional. e.g. doubling 10 -> 20 turns went from 4 to 9 paperclips
- the 30 turn one might of been 14 but one fell off when Ben sneezed
- independent var = no. of turns, dependant var = no. of paperclips, control = current (2 A), same nail, same size paperclips
- improvement: use a newtonmeter instead of paperclips bc paperclips are a bit random

ways to make an electromagnet stronger:
1. more turns on the coil
2. bigger current
3. add an iron core (soft iron bc it loses magnetism quickly)

== Uses ==
- scrapyard cranes (switch off to drop the cars)
- electric bell - current makes electromagnet pull the hammer, breaks circuit, springs back, repeat = ringing
- relay - small current in one circuit switches on a big current in another circuit. like car starter motors. safer
- MRI scanners (huge electromagnets, superconducting)
- loudspeakers (see motor effect)

== Motor effect (HIGHER) ==
wire carrying current in a magnetic field feels a FORCE. bc the two fields interact.
FLEMING'S LEFT HAND RULE:
- thumb = Force (motion)
- first finger = Field (N to S)
- second finger = current (I)
Mr Okafor's mnemonic: "Father Bought Ice-cream" -> F, B, I going thumb, first, second. (B is field, I is current)
- Fleming's left hand rule is for MOTORS (left = motor, Mr O said remember "Left = Lift off")

equation: F = B I L
F = force (N), B = magnetic flux density (tesla (T)), I = current (A), L = length of wire in the field (m)
- force is biggest when the wire is at 90 deg to the field, zero if parallel

WORKED EXAMPLE (from the board, 21st Oct):
B = 0.25 T, I = 3 A, L = 0.4 m
F = 0.25 x 3 x 0.4 = 0.3 N
(i got 3 N first bc i multiplied by 10 for some reason. DONT DO THAT)

homework q: B = 0.5 T, I = 1.2 A, L = 0.15 m -> F = 0.09 N (Mr O ticked it)

== Electric motors ==
- coil of wire on an axle in a magnetic field
- one side gets pushed up, other side pushed down -> it rotates
- split-ring commutator swaps the current direction every half turn so it keeps spinning the same way
- speed up the motor: more current, more turns, stronger magnet
- we made a mini motor with a battery, magnet and a bit of copper wire, ours spun for about 6 seconds before it fell off lol (Amira's other group's one actually worked properly)

== Loudspeakers ==
- AC through coil -> coil moves back and forth in the field of a permanent magnet -> cone vibrates -> pressure waves = sound

== extra bits ==
- Faraday did induction (generators/dynamos) - thats yr 11 / next topic, not in this test
- Mr O said write "magnetic flux density" not "magnet strength" in the exam
- 6 mark q likely on the electromagnet practical - use the data + say about control vars
- homework due Fri 3rd Nov: exam qs p. 118-119 (q 1-6)
- REMEMBER: induced magnets always attract. copper isnt magnetic. F = BIL only works for current at right angles to the field

notes.title: Biology — Cells and Microscopy
notes.text:
BIOLOGY - Cells & Microscopy  (B1, Mrs Patel)
started 18/9, test is week of 9th Oct

## Animal vs plant cells
both have:
- nucleus - contains DNA/genetic material, controls the cell
- cytoplasm - where most chemical reactions happen (jelly stuff)
- cell membrane - controls what goes in & out
- mitochondria - aerobic respiration happens here, releases energy
- ribosomes - make proteins (protein synthesis)
plant cells ALSO have:
- cell wall (cellulose) - strengthens the cell
- chloroplasts - photosynthesis, contain chlorophyll
- permanent vacuole - full of cell sap, keeps cell firm/turgid
(Mrs P: "3 extra for plants - Wall, Chloro, Vac" just learn it)

## Prokaryotes vs eukaryotes
- eukaryotic = has a nucleus (animal, plant, fungi, protists)
- prokaryotic = bacteria, NO nucleus. DNA is a single loop floating in the cytoplasm + little rings called plasmids
- bacteria are way smaller, about 1-2 µm long (some bigger)
- bacteria can have a flagellum to move
- antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first person to see bacteria w/ his homemade microscope ("animalcules" lol) in the 1670s

## The light microscope
parts: eyepiece lens, objective lenses, stage, clips, lamp, coarse focus, fine focus
- our school ones: eyepiece x10, objectives x4, x10, x40
- total mag = eyepiece x objective, so max for us = x400
- ALWAYS start on lowest power (x4) and focus with coarse knob first, then fine focus on higher ones
- never use the coarse focus on x40, you smash the slide (Ryan did this, RIP slide)

## Onion cell practical (22nd Sept)
group: "Team Mitochondria" (me, Ryan, Leah)
method:
1. peel thin layer of epidermis off the onion with tweezers
2. put on slide in a drop of water
3. add iodine solution (stains the nucleus + makes it easier to see)
4. lower coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle so no air bubbles
5. look at on x100 then x400
results: cells looked like bricks in a wall, nucleus was a little dark blob. no chloroplasts bc onion bulb is underground (no light)
- we drew 3 cells

## Cheek cells
- swab inside of cheek with cotton bud, smear on slide
- stain with methylene blue
- cells were rounder and more random shapes than onion, nucleus stained dark blue
- cheek cell about 60 µm across (Mrs P's figure on the board)
- had to put used cotton buds in disinfectant (hygiene!!)

## MAGNIFICATION
magnification = image size / actual size
Mrs Patel's way of remembering: "MIA - missing in action" -> Magnification = Image over Actual
rearrange: actual size = image size / magnification
- make sure units are the SAME before dividing!!

## Units (people lose marks on this)
- 1 mm = 1000 µm (micrometres)
- 1 µm = 1000 nm (nanometres)
- so mm -> µm x1000, µm -> nm x1000
- standard form: 1 µm = 1 x 10^-6 m, 1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m

worked out our onion cell: image in my drawing was 12 mm long at x400
actual = 12 / 400 = 0.03 mm = 30 µm (Mrs P said this is about right for onion)

## Electron microscopes
- use beams of electrons instead of light
- much higher magnification AND resolution
- resolution = ability to tell apart 2 points that are close together
- electron microscope resolution can be about 0.1 nm (transmission EM) so you can see ribosomes, inside of mitochondria etc
- light microscope cant see ribosomes at all
- BUT electron microscopes are massive, expensive, and specimen must be dead (in a vacuum)
- SEM = 3D surface image, TEM = 2D slice, higher res
- the invention of the EM in the 1930s meant we learned loads more about sub-cellular structures

## Specialised cells (p. 34 in the textbook)
- sperm cell - tail, lots of mitochondria, acrosome w/ enzymes
- nerve cell - long axon, branched dendrites to connect
- muscle cell - lots of mitochondria, can contract
- root hair cell - big surface area for absorbing water+minerals, no chloroplasts
- xylem - dead cells, hollow tubes, lignin
- phloem - sieve plates, companion cells
- cell differentiation = cell becomes specialised. animal cells mostly do it early, plant cells can do it all their life

## Drawing rules (Mrs P is STRICT)
- pencil only
- no shading!!!
- clear continuous lines
- label lines with a ruler, don't cross them
- give the magnification + title
my onion drawing got 7/10 bc i shaded the nucleus. annoying.

## Required practical exam tips
- explain why you use a stain (to make structures visible / add contrast)
- explain coverslip (keeps specimen flat, stops it drying out, protects lens)
- calculation q's: SHOW THE WORKING + units
- homework: exam q's on p. 36-37 due Mon 2nd Oct

notes.title: Chemistry — Electrolysis
notes.text:
CHEM - ELECTROLYSIS
Mr Hughes, C5. Test on 30th Jan!!!

### What is electrolysis
- splitting up an ionic compound using electricity
- the ionic compound must be MOLTEN or DISSOLVED in water (= electrolyte) so the ions can move
- solid ionic compounds dont conduct bc ions are fixed in the lattice
- electrodes: the positive one = ANODE, the negative one = CATHODE
- Mr Hughes's mnemonic: PANIC -> Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode
- positive ions (cations) go to the cathode, negative ions (anions) go to the anode
- OIL RIG - oxidation is loss (of electrons), reduction is gain
- at cathode = reduction (ions gain electrons), at anode = oxidation
- electrodes usually inert - graphite or platinum - so they don't react

### Molten compounds
- molten ionic compound -> metal at cathode, non-metal at anode. simple
- e.g. molten zinc chloride -> zinc + chlorine
- Humphry Davy discovered sodium and potassium by electrolysis in 1807 (bonus fact, Mr H loves Davy)

### Electrolysis of solutions (the annoying bit)
in water there are also H+ and OH- ions from the water
AT THE CATHODE:
- if the metal is MORE reactive than hydrogen -> hydrogen gas made
- if less reactive than hydrogen (copper, silver, gold) -> the metal is made
AT THE ANODE:
- if there's halide ions (Cl-, Br-, I-) -> the halogen is made
- if not -> oxygen is made (from the OH- ions)
- 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-

### Copper sulfate practical (9th Jan) - required practical
group: "The Bunsen Burners" (me, Tom, Priya, Kacper)
- used COPPER electrodes not graphite
- current 0.5 A for 20 minutes
- weighed electrodes before & after (dried them with propanone first)
results:
| electrode | before (g) | after (g) | change |
| cathode | 12.36 | 12.78 | +0.42 g |
| anode | 12.51 | 12.07 | -0.44 g |
- cathode gained mass bc copper deposited on it (pinky-brown coating)
- anode lost mass bc copper atoms -> Cu2+ ions went into solution
- should be the same in theory - ours were 0.02 g off, prob bc a bit of copper flaked off the anode into the bottom of the beaker
- charge: Q = I x t = 0.5 A x 1200 s = 600 C
- with graphite electrodes instead you'd get copper at cathode + oxygen at the anode and the blue colour fades

### Brine (sodium chloride solution)
- products: hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode, sodium hydroxide left in solution
- all 3 are really useful (NaOH for soap/bleach, Cl2 for water treatment & PVC, H2 for fuel / margarine)
- we did a small version with test tubes over the electrodes on 16th Jan
- our hydrogen tube filled in 3 min 40 s, the chlorine one never filled fully bc chlorine dissolves a bit in water
- TESTS:
  - hydrogen: lit splint -> squeaky pop
  - chlorine: bleaches damp blue litmus paper (goes red first then white)
  - oxygen: relights a glowing splint
- smelled like a swimming pool, Mr H opened all the windows

### Half equations (HIGHER)
- cathode: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2
- anode: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-
- copper: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu
- the electrons have to balance. Mr H: "electrons are like change from a shop, it has to add up"

### Extracting aluminium
- aluminium is more reactive than carbon so cant use carbon to reduce it, have to use electrolysis
- ore = bauxite -> purified to aluminium oxide (Al2O3)
- aluminium oxide has a really high melting point so its dissolved in molten CRYOLITE
- this means it can be done at about 950 °C - saves loads of energy & money
- cathode: Al3+ + 3e- -> Al (molten aluminium collects at the bottom)
- anode: 2O2- -> O2 + 4e-
- the anodes are made of graphite (carbon) and the oxygen reacts with them to make CO2, so they burn away and have to be replaced regularly
- uses LOADS of electricity -> expensive. smelters are often near hydroelectric power stations

### Electroplating
- coat an object in a thin layer of metal using electrolysis
- object = cathode, plating metal = anode, electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal
- e.g. silver plating cutlery, chromium on bike parts (shiny + stops rust)

### Exam stuff
- revision guide p. 156-159
- 6 markers often ask: predict products + explain. use the reactivity rules above
- Mr H's warning: dont say "the electrons move through the solution" - the IONS move in the solution, electrons move in the wires
- past paper mark (Nov mock): 19/30. need to sort out half equations

notes.title: History — World War One
notes.text:
HISTORY - WW1 (1914-1918)  Ms Bradley
GCSE Conflict & Tension unit. Knowledge test 12th Feb, essay due 26th Feb

## LONG TERM CAUSES - "MAIN"
- Militarism - arms race, esp. naval race Britain vs Germany (Dreadnoughts! Britain launched HMS Dreadnought 1906)
- Alliances - Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia) vs Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy)
- Imperialism - competing for empires/colonies, e.g. Moroccan crises
- Nationalism - pride in your country, Serbian nationalism in the Balkans
Ms Bradley adds the A for Assassination as the short term trigger so it's MAIN-A -> her mnemonic: "My Aunt Isn't Nice, Actually"

## SHORT TERM - Sarajevo
- Archduke Franz Ferdinand (heir to Austria-Hungary) shot in Sarajevo, 28 June 1914
- by Gavrilo Princip, member of the Black Hand (Serbian nationalist group)
- driver took a wrong turn after the first bomb failed, stopped right next to Princip. (sandwich story = myth, Ms B was v clear)
- Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia -> Russia mobilised to help Serbia -> Germany declared war on Russia + France
- Schlieffen Plan: Germany wanted to knock out France quickly through Belgium, then turn on Russia
- Britain joined 4 Aug 1914 bc Germany invaded Belgium (Treaty of London 1839 - "scrap of paper")

## The Western Front
- Schlieffen plan failed - Battle of the Marne Sept 1914
- "race to the sea" -> both sides dig trenches from the Channel to Switzerland
- stalemate for ~4 years

## Trenches
- front line, support trench, reserve trench, communication trenches
- no man's land in between w/ barbed wire
- conditions: rats, lice, mud, trench foot, shell shock
- trench foot = feet rot from standing in cold wet water for days, could need amputating. fixed with whale oil + dry socks + duckboards

group presentation on trench foot (5th Feb)
group: "The Tommies" (me, Harry, Zainab, Ellie)
- got 18/25, Ms B said good sources but we went over time (9 mins instead of 6...)
- Harry's bit about whale oil was the best part apparently

## New weapons
- machine guns (could fire 400-600 rounds/min)
- poison gas - chlorine first used at Ypres 1915, then phosgene, mustard gas
- tanks - first used at the Somme Sept 1916, kept breaking down
- aircraft - reconnaissance at first, then dogfights
- artillery caused most casualties

## Big battles
### Verdun
- the French one, started earlier in 1916, Germany wanted to "bleed France white"
- lasted most of the year
- one reason Britain launched the Somme = to take pressure off the French at Verdun
### The Somme
- started 1 July 1916
- Haig in charge, week-long bombardment first, was meant to destroy the wire. it didnt
- 57,470 British casualties on the FIRST DAY (about 19,000 killed)
- ended Nov 1916, Allies gained about 6 miles
- Haig = "Butcher of the Somme"? or did he learn lessons? -> interpretations q!! Ms B wants us to argue both sides
### Passchendaele 1917 - mud, mud, more mud

## 1917 - 1918
- USA joined April 1917 (unrestricted submarine warfare + Zimmermann telegram)
- Russia left after revolution - Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, March 1918
- German Spring Offensive (Ludendorff) March 1918 - nearly worked
- Hundred Days Offensive - Allies push back
- Germany asks for an armistice, fighting stops in the autumn of 1918

## Treaty of Versailles
- signed 28 June 1919 (5 years to the day after Sarajevo - Ms B says this is a nice detail to drop in)
- Big Three: Clemenceau (France), Lloyd George (Britain), Woodrow Wilson (USA)
  - Ms B: "Clem wants revenge, Lloyd wants the middle, Woody wants peace"
- terms - LAMB: Land, Army, Money, Blame
  - Land: Alsace-Lorraine back to France, lost all colonies, Polish corridor
  - Army: max 100,000 men, no air force, no tanks, 6 battleships, Rhineland demilitarised
  - Money: reparations £6.6 billion (set in 1921)
  - Blame: Article 231 war guilt clause
- Germans called it a "Diktat" (dictated peace)

## my essay
"How far was the Treaty of Versailles fair?" - got 14/20. need to use more own knowledge and actually reach a judgement (Ms B wrote "SO WHAT?" next to paragraph 2 lol)

## random extra
- my great-great-grandad was in the Durham Light Infantry, mum has his medal
- textbook p. 44-61 for this whole unit
- source q's: always do Content + Provenance (NOP = Nature, Origin, Purpose)

notes.title: Geography — Rivers and Flooding
notes.text:
GEOG - RIVERS & FLOODING
Mr Lindqvist (Physical Landscapes in the UK, paper 1)

### Drainage basin vocab
- drainage basin = area of land drained by a river + its tributaries
- watershed = the boundary of a drainage basin (usually high ground)
- source = where river starts
- mouth = where it meets the sea
- tributary = smaller river joining a bigger one
- channel = where the water actually flows

### The long profile
upper course -> middle course -> lower course
- upper: steep gradient, narrow + shallow, V-shaped valley, lots of vertical erosion, big angular boulders
- middle: gentler, wider, meanders start, lateral erosion
- lower: flat, wide + deep channel, floodplains, levees, estuaries, small smooth sediment
- discharge + velocity INCREASE downstream (people think it slows down but it doesn't, Mr L said this is a classic mistake)

### Erosion processes
Mr L mnemonic: "Happy Ants Sing Always"
- Hydraulic action - force of the water hitting the banks, air gets forced into cracks
- Abrasion - rocks carried by the river scrape the bed+banks (like sandpaper)
- Solution - some rocks (limestone/chalk) dissolve in the water
- Attrition - rocks knock into each other, get smaller + rounder

### Transportation
- traction (rolling big boulders), saltation (bouncing), suspension (carried in water), solution (dissolved)
- "Tiny Snails Sit Still" was last year's teacher's one but Mr L hates it

### Landforms
- waterfalls: hard rock on top of soft rock, soft rock erodes faster -> undercut -> overhang collapses -> plunge pool, gorge forms as it retreats. e.g. High Force, River Tees (21 m drop)
- interlocking spurs (upper course)
- meanders: fastest flow on outside bend -> erosion -> river cliff; slow flow inside -> deposition -> slip-off slope
- ox-bow lakes: neck of meander gets narrower, breaks through in a flood, deposition seals off the old loop
- levees: flood -> water loses energy -> heaviest sediment dropped first nearest the channel -> builds up

### FIELDWORK - Kettlewell Beck (18th May)
group: "Meander Mob" (me, Callum, Sophie, Ade)
hypothesis: width, depth & velocity increase downstream
| site | width (m) | avg depth (m) | velocity (m/s) |
| 1 | 2.4 | 0.18 | 0.21 |
| 2 | 3.9 | 0.27 | 0.34 |
| 3 | 5.6 | 0.42 | 0.55 |
- so velocity went from 0.21 m/s at site 1 up to 0.55 m/s at site 3
- velocity measured with a float (orange!) over 10 m, timed 3 times, took the average
- depth measured w/ metre ruler at 5 points across
- hypothesis ACCEPTED (mostly). site 2 depth a bit weird bc there was a big pool
- risk: slippy rocks, Callum fell in at site 3 (he was fine, just wet)
- evaluation: only 3 sites, float got stuck on a branch once, do more repeats

### Flood hydrographs
- shows discharge (cumecs = m3/s) vs time, with rainfall as bars
- peak rainfall -> peak discharge. gap between them = LAG TIME
- rising limb, falling limb
- the hydrograph we drew in class (made up data for "River Brennock"): lag time 9 hours, peak discharge 240 cumecs
- short lag time + high peak = flashy = more flood risk

factors that increase flood risk:
- steep slopes, impermeable rock (clay/granite), saturated soil
- urbanisation - tarmac & concrete are impermeable, drains take water straight to the river
- deforestation - less interception
- heavy/prolonged rain, snowmelt

### Case study - Boscastle, Cornwall, 16 Aug 2004
- loads of rain in a few hours over the high ground
- 2 rivers (Valency + Jordan) come together just above the village, steep narrow valley
- ~100 cars washed into the sea, buildings destroyed, no one died (helicopter rescue)
- afterwards: river channel widened + deepened, new bridge with bigger arch, car park moved

### Flood management
HARD ENGINEERING (man-made structures, expensive)
- dams + reservoirs - control discharge, can make HEP, but flood land, cost loads
- straightening the channel - water moves away faster (but floods downstream!)
- embankments - raise the banks
- flood relief channels - e.g. the Jubilee River near Maidenhead
- the Thames Barrier protects London from tidal surges
SOFT ENGINEERING (works with nature, cheaper)
- flood warnings (EA), preparation - sandbags
- floodplain zoning - don't build on the floodplain
- planting trees - afforestation increases interception
- river restoration - put the meanders back

our town's flood wall (built after the 2015 floods) cost £4.2 million - Mr L says it's protected about 300 houses since. local paper: "worth every penny"

### Exam bits
- textbook p. 88-103
- 9 mark q: "assess the costs and benefits of a flood management scheme"
- always use NAMED example + numbers
- test on 6th June, my last one was 41/60

notes.title: Maths — Ratio and Proportion
notes.text:
MATHS - Ratio & Proportion
Miss Chen, 10X2. Unit 7. Test 12 Mar

---- RATIO BASICS ----
- ratio compares amounts of things. 3:2 means "for every 3 of these theres 2 of those"
- simplify by dividing both sides by the HCF. 12:18 -> 2:3
- ratios with units -> make the units the same first!! e.g. 50p : £2 = 50:200 = 1:4
- ratio as fraction: in 3:5 the first part is 3/8 of the total (not 3/5!!! classic mistake)
- 1:n form -> divide both by the first number. e.g. 4:10 = 1:2.5

---- SHARING IN A RATIO ----
Miss Chen's mnemonic: "Angry Dogs Munch" -> Add the parts, Divide the total, Multiply
example from the board: share £84 in the ratio 3:4
- Add: 3 + 4 = 7 parts
- Divide: 84 / 7 = £12 per part
- Multiply: 3 x 12 = £36, 4 x 12 = £48
- CHECK: 36 + 48 = 84
harder one: "the ratio of boys to girls is 5:3, there are 14 more boys than girls, how many altogether?"
- difference = 5 - 3 = 2 parts = 14 -> 1 part = 7 -> total 8 parts = 56 people

---- RECIPES / SCALING ----
group project: bake sale for Year 7 charity week (group: "Ratio Rangers" - me, Mia, Hamza, Lucy)
original recipe makes 12 cupcakes:
- 150 g flour
- 120 g sugar
- 2 eggs
- 100 g butter
we needed 30 cupcakes -> scale factor 30 / 12 = 2.5
- flour 150 x 2.5 = 375 g
- sugar 120 x 2.5 = 300 g
- eggs 2 x 2.5 = 5 eggs
- butter 100 x 2.5 = 250 g
we sold out in 20 mins, made £27.50 (Hamza ate 2 tho)
- Miss C said use the "unitary method" if the numbers are awkward: find for 1 first, then times up

---- BEST BUY ----
compare price per gram (or grams per penny)
cereal example:
- 500 g for £1.85 -> 37p per 100 g
- 750 g for £2.60 -> about 34.7p per 100 g
- so the 750 g box is better value
- ALWAYS say which is better + show the comparison

---- DIRECT PROPORTION ----
- y ∝ x means y = kx (k = constant of proportionality)
- graph = straight line through the origin
- method: write y = kx, sub in values to find k, then use it
homework q: y is directly proportional to x, y = 20 when x = 8 -> k = 2.5, so when x = 14, y = 35
- can also be y ∝ x² (y = kx²) or y ∝ cube of x etc

---- INVERSE PROPORTION ----
- y ∝ 1/x means y = k/x
- as one goes up, the other goes down
- graph is a curve (doesnt touch the axes)
- e.g. 6 workers take 10 days to build a wall -> total = 60 "worker-days" -> 4 workers take 15 days
- Miss C: "more workers = less time, that's the vibe of inverse"

---- MAP SCALES ----
- scale 1:25 000 means 1 cm on the map = 25 000 cm in real life = 250 m
- so 4 cm on the map = 1 km
- our walking route on the school trip map was 7.4 cm -> 1.85 km
- the Explorer map we used for DofE was 1:25 000

---- RATIOS IN REAL LIFE ----
- gears, mixing paint, concrete (1:2:3 cement:sand:gravel)
- telly screens are 16:9
- golden ratio ≈ 1.618 (bonus, Miss C showed us the sunflower thing, not on the test)

---- RATIO <-> PERCENTAGES ----
- ratio 3:7 -> total 10 parts -> 30% and 70%
- in our class 18 people have a phone with a cracked screen and 12 don't -> 18:12 = 3:2 -> 60% cracked (Miss C was horrified)

---- EXCHANGE RATES (proportion again) ----
- exchange rate on the worksheet: £1 = €1.16
- £250 -> 250 x 1.16 = €290
- €87 -> 87 / 1.16 = £75
- Miss C: "if you're going INTO euros the number gets bigger, so times. coming back, divide"
- Lucy's family trip to Spain: she got €580 for £500 at the airport (bad rate, airports rip you off)

---- SIMILAR SHAPES ----
- similar = same shape, different size, all sides in the same ratio
- length scale factor k -> area scale factor k² -> volume scale factor k³
- e.g. two similar cylinders, heights 5 cm and 15 cm -> k = 3, so area x9, volume x27
- small one holds 40 cm³ -> big one holds 40 x 27 = 1080 cm³
- this was the q everyone got wrong in the starter on 26 Feb, most people just did x3

---- RATES ----
- speed = distance / time is a proportion thing too (distance ∝ time if speed is constant)
- Miss C's triangle for speed: "Dad's Silly Teeth" (D on top, S and T on the bottom)
- e.g. 120 km in 1.5 hours = 80 km/h
- density = mass / volume, pressure = force / area - same idea

---- MISTAKES I KEEP MAKING ----
- mixing up the order (if it says girls:boys, put girls FIRST)
- forgetting to check units
- in "share in the ratio" Qs I give the parts not the amounts - READ THE QUESTION

notes.title: Economics — Supply and Demand
notes.text:
ECONOMICS - SUPPLY & DEMAND  (Mr Adeyemi)
Theme 1, microeconomics. Topic test 20th Oct

## Markets
- market = where buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods/services (doesn't have to be a physical place, e.g. eBay)
- price mechanism allocates resources - signalling, rationing, incentive functions (Mr A: "SRI, like the country")

## DEMAND
- demand = the quantity consumers are willing AND able to buy at a given price (effective demand)
- law of demand: price up -> quantity demanded down (inverse relationship)
- demand curve slopes DOWN left to right
- movement ALONG the curve = only caused by change in the good's own price (extension / contraction)
- SHIFT of the curve = caused by anything else
Mr A's acronym for things that shift demand: PASIFIC
- Population
- Advertising
- Substitutes (price of)
- Income
- Fashion/tastes
- Interest rates
- Complements (price of)
- normal goods: income up -> demand up. inferior goods: income up -> demand down (e.g. value brand beans, bus travel?)

## SUPPLY
- supply = quantity producers are willing and able to sell at a given price
- price up -> quantity supplied up (more profitable)
- supply curve slopes UP
- shifts in supply: costs of production, tech, taxes/subsidies, weather (for agriculture), number of firms
- a tax shifts supply LEFT, a subsidy shifts it RIGHT

## EQUILIBRIUM
- where demand = supply, market clears
- excess demand (shortage) when price below equilibrium -> price rises
- excess supply (surplus) when price above -> price falls
- Alfred Marshall drew the first proper supply & demand diagram ("Marshallian cross") - Mr A loves him

### Trading game (3rd Oct)
- "pit market" - half of class were buyers, half sellers of "wheat cards", each had a secret value card
- group: "The Invisible Hands" (me, Kofi, Hannah, Will)
- round 1 prices were all over the place (£3 to £8)
- by round 4 nearly every trade was around £4.50 -> that was the equilibrium price
- Mr A's point: nobody planned it, it just happened bc of self-interest
- Kofi made the most "profit" in our group (£11), I made £6

## PRICE ELASTICITY OF DEMAND (PED)
PED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price
Mr A: "Quantity over Price - Quite Precise"
- usually negative (ignore the sign when deciding elastic/inelastic, but WRITE it)
- PED bigger than 1 (ignoring sign) -> elastic (responsive). luxuries, lots of substitutes
- less than 1 -> inelastic. necessities, addictive goods (petrol, cigarettes), few substitutes
- exactly 1 -> unitary elastic
worked example: price up 10%, quantity down 25% -> PED = -25/10 = -2.5 -> elastic
- if demand is inelastic, raising price -> total revenue goes UP
- if elastic, raising price -> total revenue goes DOWN
- revenue = price x quantity

### Our school canteen example (Mr A made us do it for homework)
- cookies went up from 80p to £1 in September (25% price rise)
- sales fell from 240 to 180 a week (25% drop)
- PED = -25/25 = -1.0 -> unitary elastic. revenue: before 240 x 80p = £192, after 180 x £1 = £180. so revenue actually went DOWN a bit (Mr A said real data is messy, % changes depend on which end you start from)
- Hannah pointed out the vending machine is a substitute

## PED factors - "SPLAT"
- Substitutes, Proportion of income, Luxury/necessity, Addictive/habit, Time period

## Exceptions / weird goods
- Giffen good - inferior good where price up leads to demand up (really rare, potatoes in Irish famine is the classic but disputed)
- speculative demand e.g. houses, bitcoin
- Mr A mentioned another type for status/luxury goods but I didnt write down the name (ask!!)

## Price controls
- maximum price (ceiling) set BELOW equilibrium -> shortages (e.g. rent controls)
- minimum price (floor) set ABOVE equilibrium -> surplus (e.g. minimum wage = unemployment in theory; minimum unit pricing on alcohol in Scotland)
- government intervention can lead to black markets

## Exam stuff
- ALWAYS draw a diagram, label axes P and Q, label curves D and S, show old and new equilibrium (P1 Q1 -> P2 Q2)
- textbook p. 61-74
- essay "Evaluate the impact of a sugar tax on the market for fizzy drinks" - got 11/15. need more evaluation (Mr A: "it depends... on WHAT?")

ENG LIT - MACBETH revision
Mrs Okonkwo, set 3. Closed book exam!! learn quotes

### Context (AO3)
- written by Shakespeare for King James I (James VI of Scotland, became king of England in 1603)
- James was obsessed with witchcraft - wrote "Daemonologie" - so witches in the play = crowd pleaser for him
- Gunpowder Plot 1605 - Catholics tried to blow up James + parliament -> play is basically anti-regicide propaganda
- Divine Right of Kings - king chosen by God, so killing a king = against God + nature
- Great Chain of Being - order of everything God -> king -> nobles -> peasants -> animals. Duncan's murder breaks it -> nature goes wrong (horses eat each other, darkness in day)
- Jacobean audiences believed in witches. women were expected to be obedient

### Plot recap (quick)
Act 1 - witches, prophecies (Thane of Cawdor, king), Lady M reads letter, plans murder
Act 2 - Macbeth kills Duncan, Malcolm & Donalbain flee
Act 3 - Banquo killed, Fleance escapes, Banquo's ghost at the banquet (3.4)
Act 4 - witches again (apparitions), Macduff's family murdered
Act 5 - Lady M sleepwalking (5.1), she dies, Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane, Macduff kills Macbeth ("not of woman born" bc he was "from his mother's womb untimely ripped" = C-section)

### THEMES
Mrs O's mnemonic: GASK - Guilt, Ambition, Supernatural, Kingship ("Macbeth runs on GASK")
- Guilt - blood imagery, hands, sleep. "Macbeth does murder sleep"
- Ambition - "vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself" (1.7) - he knows its a problem!
- Supernatural - witches, dagger, ghost. do they CAUSE it or just suggest it?
- Kingship - Duncan (good, generous) vs Macbeth (tyrant) vs Edward the Confessor (healing king) vs Malcolm

### KEY QUOTES (learn 2-3 per character)
Witches:
- "Fair is foul, and foul is fair" (1.1) - paradox, things aren't what they seem, trochaic tetrameter = sounds like a spell

- "Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?" (2.2)
- "O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!" (3.2)

Lady Macbeth:
- "Look like th'innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't" (1.5) - Genesis/Eden link
- "unsex me here" (1.5) - rejects femininity
- "A little water clears us of this deed" (2.2) -> compare with ->
- "Out, damned spot! out, I say!" (5.1) - guilt has destroyed her
Banquo:
- "oft-times, to win us to our harm, / The instruments of darkness tell us truths" (1.3)

### Characters
Macbeth - brave soldier at start ("brave Macbeth", "Bellona's bridegroom") -> tyrant, "butcher"
Lady Macbeth - dominant, manipulates by questioning his manhood, then collapses. her arc goes the OPPOSITE way to Macbeth's
Banquo - foil to Macbeth, hears the same prophecy but doesn't act
Macduff - foil, genuine grief "He has no children" / "I must also feel it as a man"
the witches - ambiguous. "weird" = from wyrd = fate

### Writing the essay

### Things to remember

notes.title: Computing — Algorithms and Sorting
notes.text:
COMPUTING - Algorithms & Sorting  (Mr Kowalski, OCR J277 2.1)

## What's an algorithm
- set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem
- computational thinking: ABSTRACTION (remove unnecessary detail), DECOMPOSITION (break into smaller problems), ALGORITHMIC THINKING
- can be shown as pseudocode or flowchart
- flowchart symbols: oval = start/stop, rectangle = process, parallelogram = input/output, diamond = decision, rectangle w/ double sides = subroutine

## SEARCHING
### Linear search
- check every item one by one from the start until you find it
- works on unsorted lists
- slow on big lists. linear search is O(n) - Mr K said we don't need Big O for GCSE but "nice to know for A level"
### Binary search
- list MUST be sorted first!!!
- look at middle item, if it's the target stop, if target is smaller -> discard right half, if bigger -> discard left half, repeat
- much faster on big lists
- for 1000 items max comparisons = 10 (bc 2^10 = 1024)
- Mr K: "binary search is like the guessing game, higher or lower"
### Search worked example (from the board)
list: [3, 8, 12, 19, 23, 31, 40, 47, 56]
find 40 with binary search:
- middle = 23 (index 4), 40 > 23 -> discard the left half
- left with [31, 40, 47, 56], take the lower middle = 40 -> found!
- 2 comparisons. linear search would have needed 7
- Mr K said either middle is fine if you round the same way every time

## SORTING
### Bubble sort
- go through list comparing adjacent pairs, swap if in wrong order
- after each pass the biggest one "bubbles" to the end
- repeat passes until a pass with no swaps
- easy to code but slow (inefficient) on big lists
- good thing: doesn't need extra memory

### Unplugged activity (people sort!) - 3rd Feb
8 of us stood in a line holding numbers: 7, 3, 9, 1, 5, 8, 2, 6
- did bubble sort physically, Mr K counted
- took 15 swaps total to sort it
- Ollie kept swapping when he shouldn't lol
- then did merge sort in groups of 2 -> 4 -> 8, it was way less chaotic

### Merge sort
- divide and conquer
- split list in half repeatedly until each sub-list has 1 item
- then merge pairs back together in order
- Mr K's mnemonic: "Don't Cry, Code" -> Divide, Conquer, Combine
- faster than bubble on big lists but uses more memory (all the sublists)
- trace for [6, 2, 9, 4]: split -> [6, 2] [9, 4] -> [6] [2] [9] [4] -> merge -> [2, 6] [4, 9] -> [2, 4, 6, 9]
- invented by John von Neumann in 1945 (Mr K's fun fact)

### Insertion sort
- take each item in turn and insert it into the right place in the sorted part on the left
- like sorting a hand of cards
- efficient on small lists or lists that are nearly sorted
- trace example (from the worksheet):
  [5, 2, 4, 1]
  -> [2, 5, 4, 1]
  -> [2, 4, 5, 1]
  -> [1, 2, 4, 5]

## Python timing experiment (10th Feb)
group "Byte Me" (me, Ollie, Saanvi)
- wrote bubble sort + merge sort in Python, used the time module to time them on a random list
- 1000 items: bubble sort 0.087 s, merge sort 0.004 s
- 5000 items: bubble 2.31 s (!!), merge 0.021 s
- conclusion: bubble gets massively worse as list gets bigger, merge barely changes
- Saanvi tried 20 000 for bubble and it took ages so we gave up
- Python also has a built-in .sort() which was even faster than our merge sort (Mr K said it's written in C so not a fair comparison)

## Pseudocode (OCR exam reference language)
bubble sort:
  for i = 0 to len - 2
    for j = 0 to len - 2 - i
      if list[j] > list[j+1] then
        temp = list[j]
        list[j] = list[j+1]
        list[j+1] = temp
      endif
    next j
  next i
- in the exam you can write any pseudocode as long as its clear, but OCR's is safest
- homework: write insertion sort in Python, due 17th Feb (I did it with a while loop, Mr K said fine)

## Comparing them (exam table)
| | bubble | merge | insertion |
| speed (big list) | slow | fast | slow |
| memory | low | high | low |
| easy to code | yes | no | fairly |

## Exam tips
- "describe" a sort = say the steps; "show" = actually write out each pass
- they always give a list of ~6-8 items and ask you to show bubble sort first pass - practice!!!
- trace tables: one column per variable, new row each time something changes
- revision guide p. 129-135
- mock (Jan): 41/60, dropped marks on merge sort diagram (didn't show the split stage)

HEALTH & PE THEORY - NUTRITION AND DIET
Ms Rahman. Topic 4. quiz on 23rd Jan

== The 7 nutrients ==
Ms R's mnemonic: "Carrots Fry Pretty Very Many Fish Wobbling"
1. Carbohydrates - main energy source. simple (sugars) and complex (starch - pasta, bread, rice, potatoes). should be about half of your energy
2. Fats - energy store, insulation, protects organs, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). saturated (animal fat, butter) vs unsaturated (oils, nuts, oily fish)
3. Protein - growth & repair of muscles/tissue. meat, fish, eggs, beans, lentils. made of amino acids
4. Vitamins - needed in small amounts.
   - vit A - eyesight (night vision)
   - vitamin C - healthy skin, immune system. deficiency = scurvy (sailors! bleeding gums)
   - vit D - helps absorb calcium, from sunlight. deficiency = rickets (soft bendy bones)
5. Minerals - calcium (bones & teeth), iron (red blood cells - lack of it = anaemia, tired all the time)
6. Fibre - keeps digestive system moving, prevents constipation. wholegrains, fruit & veg
7. Water - ~6-8 glasses a day (NHS), more if exercising. dehydration = headaches, poor concentration

== Energy ==
- energy in food measured in kcal (or kJ, 1 kcal = 4.2 kJ)
- per gram: fat = 9 kcal, carbs = 4 kcal, protein = 4 kcal
- so fatty foods are really "energy dense"
- guideline for men is 2,500 kcal a day (forgot to write down the women's one, ask Ms R)
- teenagers need more bc growing + more active
- energy balance: in > out -> weight gain, in < out -> weight loss

== My food diary (3 days, 8th-10th Jan) ==
- average 2,140 kcal/day
- sugar: 78 g/day average!!! recommended max free sugars for 11+ is 30 g. so I'm way over (it was the energy drinks + cereal)
- fibre only about 14 g/day (should be 30 g for adults)
- fruit & veg portions: 3/day avg (should be 5)
- Ms R's comment: "swap the fizzy drinks first, easiest win"

== Food tests practical (16th Jan) ==
group: "Five a Day Crew" (me, Jordan, Aisha, Max)
| test | for | positive result |
| Benedict's (heat in water bath) | sugar (glucose) | blue -> brick red |
| Biuret | protein | blue -> purple |
| Iodine | starch | orange -> blue-black |
| Ethanol emulsion | lipids (fats) | cloudy white layer |
our results:
- glucose drink -> brick red
- crisps -> lipid positive (cloudy) + starch positive
- egg white -> purple (protein)
- apple -> went green/yellow with Benedict's = some sugar
- Max dropped the iodine on his shirt, it stained
- safety: goggles, Benedict's needs a water bath NOT a direct flame

== Eatwell Guide ==
- fruit & veg = about a third of what you eat
- starchy carbs = just over a third
- protein ~ 12%
- dairy ~ 8%
- oils/spreads - tiny, use sparingly
- foods high in fat/salt/sugar = outside the plate, eat less often
- salt max 6 g a day for adults (about 1 teaspoon)

== Diet and health problems ==
- obesity -> type 2 diabetes, heart disease, some cancers, joint problems
- too much saturated fat -> cholesterol up -> arteries clog
- too much salt -> high blood pressure
- malnutrition = wrong balance (can be over OR under)
- anorexia / eating disorders - mental health link

== BMI ==
BMI = mass (kg) / height squared (m2)
worked example (from the board): 60 kg, 1.65 m tall
- 1.65 x 1.65 = 2.7225
- 60 / 2.7225 = 22.04 -> BMI = 22.0 (healthy range 18.5-24.9)
- under 18.5 = underweight, 25-29.9 = overweight, 30+ = obese
- problem with BMI: doesn't account for muscle (rugby players come out as "overweight")

== Special diets ==
- vegetarian (no meat/fish) / vegan (no animal products at all) - need to plan protein (beans, tofu, lentils) + iron
- coeliac disease - can't eat gluten (wheat, barley, rye)
- diabetics - watch sugar + carbs, regular meals
- religious diets - halal, kosher, some Hindus don't eat beef
- allergies - nuts, shellfish, eggs. Jordan carries an EpiPen (anaphylaxis = emergency, call 999)
- lactose intolerance - can't digest the sugar in milk properly

== Sport & diet ==
- carb loading before endurance events (marathon) - pasta the night before
- protein after training for repair
- timing: don't eat a massive meal right before exercise (blood goes to the gut)
- hydration: weigh before & after, drink to replace

== Exam/quiz bits ==
- textbook p. 72-85
- know deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets, anaemia)
- quiz 23rd Jan: 17/20 (got confused about which vitamin needs sunlight)

notes.title: Civics — How Laws Are Made
notes.text:
CITIZENSHIP - HOW LAWS ARE MADE (UK)
Mr Fairweather. Theme B: Democracy at work. test 21st Mar

### Who makes laws
- Parliament = House of Commons + House of Lords + the Monarch ("the Crown in Parliament")
- House of Commons: 650 MPs, each elected for a constituency, First Past the Post
- House of Lords: unelected - life peers, hereditary peers, 26 bishops ("Lords Spiritual")
- government = the party (or parties) with a majority in the Commons, PM + cabinet
- legislature (makes laws) vs executive (runs the country) vs judiciary (interprets laws, courts)
- separation of powers - not fully separated in UK bc ministers sit in parliament

### Where bills come from
- government bills - most bills, from manifesto promises, announced in the King's Speech
- private members' bills - from backbench MPs, chosen by ballot (20 a session), most fail due to lack of time
- ten minute rule bills - MP gets 10 mins to make the case, mostly publicity
- green paper = consultation, white paper = firm proposals
- public bill vs private bill (private = affects a specific org / place)

### STAGES OF A BILL (learn in order!!!)
Mr F's mnemonic: "Fat Squirrels Can't Resist Treats"
1. First reading - title read out, no debate, formality
2. Second reading - main debate on the general principles, vote
3. Committee stage - public bill committee goes through line by line, amendments
4. Report stage - amendments reported back to whole House, more changes
5. Third reading - final debate, no major changes, vote
-> then goes to the OTHER house (Lords) and does the same stages
-> "ping-pong" - bill goes back and forth if they disagree on amendments
-> Royal Assent - monarch signs it off, becomes an Act of Parliament
- Royal Assent is basically automatic now - it hasn't been refused in centuries

### Power of the Lords
- Parliament Act 1911 - Lords lost veto on money bills, can only delay other bills
- Parliament Act 1949 - reduced the delay to about a year
- Salisbury Convention - Lords dont block manifesto promises
- Lords are good at scrutiny - lots of experts (doctors, judges, scientists)

### Mock parliament (7th March)
- our class bill: "School Uniform (Hoodies) Bill" - allow school hoodies instead of blazers
- group "The Backbenchers" wrote it (me, Ellis, Nadia, Josh K)
- I was the minister who introduced it at second reading
- Ellis moved an amendment to only allow hoodies in winter -> rejected
- final vote: passed 17 votes to 11 (Mr F was the Speaker and kept shouting "ORDER")
- Mr F said our committee stage was too short, real ones take weeks

### Trip to Parliament (12th June)
- our tour guide was called Priya
- saw the Commons chamber - green benches. Lords - red benches
- the 2 red lines on the Commons floor are 2 sword-lengths apart (myth-ish, guide said its a good story)
- visited Westminster Hall - oldest bit, 1097
- MPs vote by walking through division lobbies ("aye" lobby / "no" lobby), takes about 15 mins

### Types of law
- statute law = Acts of Parliament (e.g. Climate Change Act 2008, Equality Act 2010)
- common law / case law = made by judges' decisions (precedent)
- secondary / delegated legislation = ministers make detailed rules under powers from an Act (statutory instruments)
- EU law used to apply, after Brexit some was "retained"
- civil law vs criminal law (different from the above - it's about the type of case)

### Devolution
- some powers given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
- Scottish Parliament - 129 MSPs, Holyrood, can make laws on health, education etc
- Welsh Senedd, Northern Ireland Assembly (Stormont) - also make some laws
- reserved matters (defence, foreign policy) stay with Westminster

### How citizens can influence laws
- contacting your MP, petitions (100k signatures -> considered for debate), campaigning, protests, pressure groups, voting
- e.g. Helen's Law, Owen's Law - campaigns by families

### exam stuff
- textbook p. 140-151
- 8 marker: "evaluate the role of the House of Lords"
- test (21st Mar) - got 26/30

notes.title: Earth Science — Volcanoes
notes.text:
EARTH SCIENCE - VOLCANOES
Dr Whitfield. unit 3 "Restless Earth". test 14 Nov

## Structure of the Earth
- crust (thin, 5-70 km), mantle (semi-molten, convection currents), outer core (liquid iron/nickel), inner core (solid, v hot)
- tectonic plates move a few cm a year - convection currents in the mantle + slab pull + ridge push

## Plate boundaries
- constructive (divergent) - plates move apart, magma rises, new crust. e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland
- destructive (convergent) - oceanic plate subducts under continental (denser), melts, magma rises -> explosive volcanoes. e.g. Andes, Japan
- conservative - plates slide past, NO volcanoes, earthquakes only. e.g. San Andreas
- hotspots - volcanoes in the middle of a plate where a mantle plume rises, e.g. Hawaii

## Types of volcano
### Shield volcanoes
- runny (low viscosity) basaltic lava, low silica
- gentle slopes, wide base, frequent but gentle eruptions
- found at constructive boundaries + hotspots
- e.g. Mauna Loa (Hawaii) - biggest volcano on Earth by volume
### Composite (strato) volcanoes
- sticky (high viscosity) andesitic/rhyolitic lava, high silica
- steep sides, layers of ash + lava, violent eruptions
- destructive boundaries
- e.g. Mt St Helens, Mt Fuji
Dr W's thing to remember: "Sticky Silica = Scary" (and runny = basalt = boring)

## Lava types (table from the board)
| lava | silica | temp | viscosity |
| basaltic | low (~50%) | ~1200 °C | runny |
| andesitic | medium | ~1000 °C | medium |
| rhyolitic | high (~70%) | ~800 °C | very sticky |
- more silica = more viscous = gas gets trapped = pressure builds = BOOM

## Viscosity practical (3rd Oct)
group: "Magma Maniacs" (me, Leon, Freya, Dev)
- timed liquids flowing down a 30 cm ramp at the same angle (20 deg)
| liquid | time (s) |
| water | 0.6 |
| washing up liquid | 9.2 |
| honey | 31 |
| golden syrup | 48 |
- golden syrup took 48 s, slowest = most viscous = like rhyolitic lava
- then honey warmed in hot water went way faster (12 s) -> shows hotter lava is runnier
- Leon got syrup all over the ramp, took ages to clean

## Eruption products
- lava flows, ash clouds, volcanic bombs, gas (SO2, CO2, water vapour), lahars (mudflows)
- pyroclastic flows - mix of hot gas, ash, rock, can go 100s of km/h (Dr W said up to 700 km/h), 1000 °C. deadliest thing
- VEI = Volcanic Explosivity Index 0-8, logarithmic (each step ~10x bigger)

## Case study 1 - Mt St Helens, USA
- erupted 18 May 1980
- bulge on north side grew ~1.5 m a day before it blew
- landslide -> lateral blast sideways
- VEI 5
- ash fell over 11 states, forests flattened
- the eruption was a big reason the US increased volcano monitoring

## Case study 2 - Eyjafjallajokull, Iceland 2010
- under a glacier -> melting ice + magma = explosive, fine ash
- ash cloud closed European airspace for ~6 days, 100,000 flights cancelled
- local farmers had to evacuate, livestock problems
- Iceland gets lots of geothermal energy from its volcanoes (positive!)

## Case study 3 - Montserrat (my homework one)
- Soufriere Hills, started 1995
- capital Plymouth buried, now abandoned. south of the island = exclusion zone
- 1997 pyroclastic flow killed 19 people
- about 2/3 of the population left the island (lots to the UK)

## Effects - primary vs secondary
- primary = straight away from the eruption itself (lava, ash fall, pyroclastic flows, gas)
- secondary = happen later as a result (lahars, fires, homelessness, disease, crop failure, jobs + tourism lost)
- Dr W wants "PEEPS" in long answers: Primary, Economic, Environmental, People, Secondary

## Supervolcanoes
- e.g. Yellowstone (USA), VEI 8, huge caldera instead of a cone
- last big eruption about 640,000 years ago
- would cover a lot of the US in ash + cause global cooling (ash + SO2 block sunlight)

## Monitoring & prediction
- seismometers - lots of small earthquakes = magma moving
- tiltmeters - ground swelling
- gas sensors - more SO2 = magma near surface
- satellites (thermal imaging), GPS
- can't predict exact time but can warn -> evacuation
- Dr W: "Prediction saves lives, protection saves property"

## Why do people live near volcanoes?
- fertile soil (weathered ash), geothermal energy, tourism, mining (sulfur, minerals), lived there for generations
- Naples ~3 million people near Vesuvius

## Exam stuff
- textbook p. 58-71
- learn 2 named examples with facts + figures
- test 14 Nov -> got 33/40

notes.title: Physics — Space and the Solar System
notes.text:
PHYSICS - SPACE & THE SOLAR SYSTEM
Ms Delacroix, P8 (separate science only). test 15th Nov

---- Our solar system ----
- Sun = a star, at the centre, 99.8% of the mass of the solar system
- 8 planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
- Ms D's planet mnemonic: "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming"
- inner 4 = rocky, outer 4 = gas/ice giants
- dwarf planets - Pluto (demoted in 2006, our group name is a protest lol), Ceres, Eris
- asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter
- moons = natural satellites orbiting planets. artificial satellites = man-made
- comets - ice + dust, very elliptical orbits, tail always points away from the Sun

---- How the solar system formed ----
- started as a nebula (cloud of dust + gas), gravity pulled it together
- most of the material went to the centre -> got hot + dense enough for fusion -> the Sun
- leftover material in a spinning disc clumped together -> planets, moons, asteroids
- rocky planets near the Sun bc it was too hot for ices to stay solid there

---- Scale model on the field (4th Oct) ----
group: "Team Pluto Was Robbed" (me, Nico, Imogen, Raf)
- Sun = a football (about 22 cm wide)
- Earth = a peppercorn 23 m from the football
- Jupiter = a grape-ish, 120 m away
- Neptune ended up 690 m away - off past the car park, Raf had to walk it with the trundle wheel
- lesson: space is mostly EMPTY. you'd need about 6000 km for the nearest star on this scale

---- Gravity & weight ----
- W = m x g
- Earth g = 9.8 N/kg (we use 9.8 not 10 in Ms D's class)
- Moon g = 1.6 N/kg
- Jupiter g = about 25 N/kg
- worked example: 55 kg person on the Moon -> W = 55 x 1.6 = 88 N (on Earth 539 N)
- mass doesn't change, weight does!!

---- Orbits ----
- gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps things in circular orbits
- the velocity is constantly changing (direction changes) even if speed is constant -> it's accelerating
- closer orbit = faster speed needed to stay in orbit
- geostationary satellites - orbit once every 24 hours above the equator, stay over the same spot -> used for TV/comms
- polar orbit satellites - low, fast, pass over the poles, used for weather & mapping, orbit every couple of hours
- if speed increases, radius must decrease to stay in a stable orbit (HIGHER)

---- Life cycle of stars ----
ALL stars start as a NEBULA (cloud of dust + gas) -> gravity pulls it together -> protostar -> gets hot enough for fusion of hydrogen into helium -> MAIN SEQUENCE star (stable bc outward pressure from fusion balances inward gravity)
small stars (like our Sun):
-> red giant -> white dwarf -> black dwarf
big stars (much more massive than the Sun):
-> red supergiant -> SUPERNOVA -> neutron star OR black hole (if really massive)
- elements heavier than iron are made in supernovas - "we're all made of star stuff" (Ms D quoting Carl Sagan, she got emotional lol)
- Sun's core is about 15 million °C
- the Sun is about 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its main sequence stage

---- Distances ----
- light-year = distance light travels in a year (about 9.5 trillion km)
- nearest star after the Sun = Proxima Centauri, light from it takes 4.2 years to reach us
- speed of light 3 x 10^8 m/s
- AU = astronomical unit, average Earth-Sun distance (~150 million km)

---- Red-shift & the Big Bang ----
- light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum = wavelength increased
- further away galaxies = more red-shift = moving away faster
- -> universe is expanding -> evidence for the Big Bang
- Big Bang: universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region about 13.8 billion years ago
- CMBR (cosmic microwave background radiation) = other evidence, leftover radiation from the early universe
- dark matter + dark energy - we don't know what they are (Ms D: "anyone who works it out gets a Nobel")

---- Exam bits ----
- textbook p. 241-255
- 6 mark: describe life cycle of a star (do BOTH paths!!)
- they sometimes ask why scientists' ideas changed - new evidence (e.g. CMBR found 1965)
- test 15th Nov -> 29/35. lost marks forgetting "fusion" in the main sequence explanation

notes.title: Biology — The Heart and Circulation
notes.text:
BIOLOGY - HEART & CIRCULATION
Mr Brennan, B4 Organisation. test 6th March

## The circulatory system
- heart + blood vessels + blood
- DOUBLE circulatory system in humans:
  - pulmonary circuit: heart -> lungs -> heart (picks up oxygen)
  - systemic circuit: heart -> body -> heart
- double bc blood goes through the heart twice per full lap. higher pressure to the body = faster delivery
- fish have a single circulation (Mr B mentioned it, prob won't come up)
- history bit: Galen thought blood was made in the liver and got used up - wrong for like 1400 years

## Structure of the heart
- 4 chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle
- atria on top (receive blood), ventricles at the bottom (pump blood out)
- RIGHT side = deoxygenated blood, LEFT side = oxygenated
- remember the diagram is flipped (like looking at someone facing you)!!
- valves stop backflow: tricuspid (right), bicuspid/mitral (left), semilunar valves in the arteries
- Mr B's mnemonic: "LAB RAT" -> Left Atrium Bicuspid, Right Atrium Tricuspid
- septum = wall between left & right sides

blood route (learn this order):
vena cava -> right atrium -> right ventricle -> pulmonary artery -> LUNGS -> pulmonary vein -> left atrium -> left ventricle -> aorta -> BODY
- pulmonary artery is the only artery w/ deoxygenated blood, pulmonary vein the only vein w/ oxygenated
- coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen

## Heart dissection (6th Feb)
group: "Ventricle Vandals" (me, Sam, Nell, Oscar)
- lamb's heart from the butcher
- cut through to see chambers, poked a glass rod through the aorta
- measured wall thickness with a ruler:
  - left ventricle wall 14 mm
  - right ventricle wall 5 mm
- left is thicker bc it pumps blood all round the body (higher pressure), right only to lungs
- could see the "heart strings" (tendons holding valves)
- Oscar nearly fainted, Nell loved it

## Natural pacemaker
- group of cells in the right atrium (SA node) sets the resting heart rate
- artificial pacemaker = electrical device implanted to correct irregular heartbeat

## Pulse practical (13th Feb)
- measured pulse at wrist (radial) for 15 s x 4
- mine: resting 72 bpm, after 2 min skipping 128 bpm
- recovery time back to resting: 3 min 20 s
- Sam's resting was 58 bpm (he does cross country) and he recovered in under 2 mins
- fitter = lower resting HR + faster recovery

## Blood vessels
| | artery | vein | capillary |
| carries | away from heart | towards heart | between |
| wall | thick, muscular, elastic | thin | one cell thick |
| lumen | narrow | wide | tiny |
| pressure | high | low | low |
| valves | no | yes | no |
- capillaries - exchange of substances by diffusion, very close to cells
- "Arteries = Away" (Mr B)

## Blood
- plasma (~55%) - yellow liquid, carries CO2, urea, glucose, hormones, proteins
- red blood cells - carry oxygen (haemoglobin), no nucleus, biconcave disc = big surface area
- white blood cells - fight infection: phagocytes engulf pathogens, lymphocytes make antibodies
- platelets - fragments of cells, help blood clot

## Cardiac output (HIGHER / sport crossover)
cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume
worked example: 72 bpm x 70 ml = 5,040 ml/min
- stroke volume = volume pumped out per beat
- during exercise both go up

## Coronary heart disease (CHD)
- fatty deposits build up in coronary arteries -> narrow -> less oxygen to heart muscle -> heart attack
- risk factors: smoking, high fat diet, lack of exercise, high BP, genetics
- treatments:
  - stents - mesh tube keeps artery open (surgery risk, but quick recovery)
  - statins - lower blood cholesterol (side effects, have to take for life)
  - transplant - donor heart, need to take immunosuppressants, waiting lists
  - artificial heart - temporary while waiting for a donor
- faulty valves -> replaced with mechanical or biological (pig/cow) valves

## Exam stuff
- textbook p. 98-109
- label the heart diagram - ALWAYS practice (the left/right flip gets everyone)
- calculation q's: show formula first
- test 6th March: 24/28!!

notes.title: History — The Space Race
notes.text:
HISTORY - THE SPACE RACE (Cold War unit)
Mr Haddad. part of Superpower Relations. quiz 22nd March

## Why was there a space race?
- Cold War - USA vs USSR, capitalism vs communism, couldn't fight directly (nukes) so competed in other ways
- space = prestige + propaganda + military (rockets that go to space can also carry nuclear warheads -> ICBMs)
- both sides used captured German rocket scientists after WW2 (USA got Wernher von Braun - V2 rocket guy)

## Soviet "firsts"
Mr H's mnemonic for the order: "Silly Little Goats Travel"
- Sputnik 1 - first artificial satellite, 4 October 1957. just beeped. Americans could hear it on radios -> PANIC ("Sputnik crisis")
- Laika - first animal to orbit Earth, Sputnik 2, Nov 1957. didn't survive :(
- Gagarin - Yuri Gagarin, first human in space, 12 April 1961, Vostok 1, one orbit, 108 minutes
- Tereshkova - Valentina Tereshkova, first woman in space, 1963
- also: first spacewalk - Alexei Leonov 1965

## US response
- NASA set up in 1958 (Eisenhower)
- National Defense Education Act - more money for science + maths in schools
- John Glenn - first American to orbit the Earth, Feb 1962 (Friendship 7)
- "missile gap" - fear the USSR was ahead (it wasn't really)

## Kennedy & the Moon
- May 1961 - JFK tells Congress the US will land a man on the Moon before the end of the decade
- Rice University speech, Sept 1962: "We choose to go to the Moon... not because they are easy, but because they are hard"
- source analysis on this speech (homework) - got 7/8. Mr H said I nailed provenance but should mention the Cold War tension right before the Cuban Missile Crisis (Oct 1962)

## Project Mercury -> Gemini -> Apollo
- Mercury - 1 person capsules
- Gemini - 2 people, practised docking + spacewalks
- Apollo - 3 people, to the Moon
- Apollo 1 (1967) - fire on the launch pad, 3 astronauts died
- Apollo 8 (Dec 1968) - first humans to orbit the Moon, "Earthrise" photo

## Apollo 11
- launched 16 July 1969, landed 20 July 1969
- Neil Armstrong first person on the Moon: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind"
- Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module
- watched by about 600 million people on TV
- US basically "won" the race to the Moon

## Cost
- Apollo programme cost about $25.4 billion (Mr H's figure - he said today that's well over $200 billion)
- NASA got about 4.4% of the federal budget in 1966 (peak)
- critics: money should have gone on poverty, civil rights, Vietnam was also costing loads

## Class debate (15th March) - "Who won the Space Race?"
- our group "Team Vostok" (me, Lily, Arjun, Theo) argued the USSR won (all the firsts!)
- other team "Team Eagle" argued USA (Moon landing = the big prize)
- we won 3-2 on the judges' votes (judges = Mr H + 4 kids from Year 12)
- Arjun's point about the USSR being first at basically everything except the Moon won it

## Later events
- Apollo 13 (1970) - oxygen tank exploded, "Houston, we've had a problem", crew got home safely
- Apollo-Soyuz (July 1975) - US + Soviet spacecraft docked, astronauts shook hands -> detente
- after that: space shuttle (USA), space stations (Salyut, Mir), later the ISS (cooperation!)

## Key people (Mr H says name drop them)
- Sergei Korolev - the Soviet "Chief Designer", his name was kept secret until he died in 1966
- Wernher von Braun - designed the Saturn V rocket that took Apollo to the Moon
- Khrushchev - used every Soviet first as propaganda ("look how advanced communism is")
- Kennedy - turned the Moon into a national goal, assassinated Nov 1963 so never saw it happen
- Johnson + Nixon - kept the funding going (Nixon phoned the astronauts on the Moon)

## Significance
- propaganda win for each side at different times
- tech spin-offs: satellites, computers, materials
- shows the Cold War was fought through competition not just weapons

## Exam bits
- revision guide p. 77-80
- "explain the importance of..." questions -> 2 consequences, each with detail
- essay "How far was the Moon landing the most important event of the Space Race?" -> 19/25. Mr H: "great detail, judgement a bit weak"

notes.title: Chemistry — Water Treatment
notes.text:
CHEMISTRY - WATER TREATMENT
Mr Hughes, C10 Using Resources. quiz 15th March

## Key words
- pure water = ONLY water molecules, nothing else (chemistry meaning, not the advert meaning)
- potable water = safe to drink. NOT pure - has dissolved salts/minerals in it, but low levels of microbes + harmful stuff
- test if water is pure: boils at exactly 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C, leaves no residue when evaporated
- Mr H: "pure isn't potable, potable isn't pure. write it on your hand"

## Where does our drinking water come from?
- UK: rain -> collects as surface water (lakes, rivers, reservoirs) or groundwater (aquifers - water in porous rock underground)
- in the south east more groundwater is used, in the north/Scotland more surface water

## Treating fresh water -> potable water
Mr H's mnemonic for the stages: "Some Silly Fish Can't Dance"
1. Screening - remove big objects (twigs, leaves, the odd shopping trolley)
2. Sedimentation - let solids settle in big tanks (sometimes add aluminium sulfate to clump small bits together = flocculation)
3. Filtration - pass through beds of sand + gravel to remove small solid particles
4. Chlorination - kill microbes (bacteria). can also use ozone or UV light
5. Distribution - pumped to homes through pipes
- Mr H said tap water has about 0.5 mg per litre chlorine left in it so it stays safe in the pipes
- some areas add fluoride (1 ppm) to help teeth - this is controversial (debate in class, Jake went off on one)

## Desalination
- when there isn't enough fresh water -> use seawater
- method 1: distillation - boil seawater, collect + condense the steam
- method 2: reverse osmosis - push seawater through membranes at high pressure
- both need LOADS of energy -> expensive. used in places like the Middle East
- the leftover salty brine can harm marine life when pumped back

## Distillation practical (23rd Nov) - required practical
group: "H2Oh No" (me, Jake, Mei, Rhys)
- analysed + purified a sample of salty water
- started with 100 cm³ of salty water
- checked pH first with universal indicator - it was neutral-ish (green)
- heated in a flask, steam went through a Liebig condenser (cold water in at the bottom, out at the top!)
- thermometer at the side arm read 100.5 °C (prob not calibrated well / bit of impurity)
- collected 62 cm³ of distillate in 25 mins
- evaporated a separate sample to dryness -> salt crystals left, mass 3.1 g from a smaller sample
- tested distillate with a few drops of silver nitrate - no white precipitate = no chloride = pure
- safety: anti-bumping granules, don't let it boil dry, goggles

## Waste water (sewage) treatment
- waste water from homes, industry, farms
- needs treating to remove organic matter + harmful microbes before going back into rivers
- industrial waste water may also need harmful chemicals removed
stages:
1. screening + grit removal
2. sedimentation -> produces sewage sludge (bottom) + effluent (top liquid)
3. effluent -> aerobic biological treatment (air pumped through, bacteria break down organic stuff)
4. sludge -> anaerobic digestion -> makes biogas (methane) for energy + digested sludge used as fertiliser
- treated effluent released back into the river

## Field trip - Riverside Sewage Works (8th March)
- our guide was called Dave, he'd worked there 27 years
- the plant treats 45 million litres a day for about 200,000 people
- the smell was AWFUL near the sludge tanks, fine near the end
- they make enough biogas to power most of the site
- we took water samples from 2 places:
  - tap water (school): pH 7.2
  - river sample (downstream): pH 6.8, slightly cloudy
- Dave said the main things they test the outflow for are ammonia + how much oxygen bacteria use up (BOD)

## Comparing
- getting potable water from fresh water is easiest + cheapest (UK)
- sewage treatment needs more processes than fresh water treatment
- desalination most expensive (energy)

## Exam stuff
- textbook p. 188-193
- describe the distillation practical step by step (6 marker - likely!!)
- don't say "chlorine cleans the water" -> say it KILLS MICROBES/bacteria
- quiz 15th March: 31/36
